papers.title: Locus-restricted genetic overlap between pelvic organ prolapse and estimated bone mineral density at 18q21.1 (SMAD7), with unresolved regulatory direction
papers.abstract: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is highly prevalent in parous women. Observational studies link POP with low bone mineral density (BMD), but shared genetic determinants are unclear. Global Mendelian randomization has not supported a causal effect of BMD on POP. We therefore asked whether overlap exists at specific loci. We merged 2,524 genome-wide significant FinnGen R12 POP variants (23,074 cases, 130,160 controls) into 30 loci, seven of which lay within 500 kb of an instrument for estimated BMD (eBMD). The clearest example is 18q21.1: lead variant rs4939832 (G allele) was associated with POP ({beta} = 0.071, P = 9.5 x 10-9) and with eBMD ({beta} = 0.018 per SD, P = 1.3 x 10-11) at the same allele. Regional colocalisation gave a posterior probability of 0.98 for signal sharing under the single-causal-variant assumption. LD-aware fine-mapping then resolved two adjacent independent causal signals with no overlapping credible sets (rs4939832 versus rs2337106; r{superscript 2} = 0.21). We then queried rs4939832 against SMAD7 in 28 blood and immune-cell eQTL analyses. No analysis reached nominal significance (minimum P = 0.118; pooled P = 0.78). Analyses within a panel are not statistically independent. Interrogating the closest target-adjacent tissues (GTEx vagina, n = 141; uterus, n = 129) likewise returned no significant cis-association (P = 0.26 and 0.77), so any cis-regulatory effect of this variant is likely small and its directionality cannot be reliably inferred from available tissue resources. Supporting evidence from independent cohorts was limited: the variant showed only nominal association in UK Biobank POP (P = 0.058) and was not assayed in the largest POP GWAS. POP and eBMD therefore overlap in a locus-restricted manner rather than through a systemic bone-mass pathway, and the cis-regulatory direction of rs4939832 remains unresolved. Functional interpretation requires well-powered eQTL data from genuine pelvic-floor connective-tissue compartments, which are not publicly available.

papers.title: Biased and variable: pictorial blood loss estimates from photographs of used menstrual pads compared with alkaline hematin
papers.abstract: STUDY QUESTION: How accurate and how variable are lay raters' estimates of menstrual blood loss when they apply a pictorial blood loss assessment chart (PBLAC) to photographs of used pads? SUMMARY ANSWER: Raters captured only about 62% of the blood measured by alkaline hematin, classified only 47.1% of their ratings of heavy cycles as heavy and gave estimates that varied substantially between raters and between sessions. WHAT IS KNOWN ALREADY: Pictorial charts are widely used to estimate menstrual blood loss, but their accuracy against alkaline hematin varies, and it is unclear how consistently different people score the same product. STUDY DESIGN, SIZE, DURATION: Cross-sectional online study of reliability and agreement with a repeated assessment, conducted in November 2026 according to a written protocol. PARTICIPANTS/MATERIALS, SETTING, METHODS: Sixty-nine women recruited through social media rated photographs of the same 117 used pads from eight cycles of a validation study in which every pad had been measured by alkaline hematin, and 44 repeated the ratings about 2 weeks later. The pad users' own in-hand scores served as a comparator. MAIN RESULTS AND THE ROLE OF CHANCE: Raters' cycle estimates captured 62% (95% CI 60-65%) of the alkaline hematin volume (mean bias -44.1 ml; 95% limits of agreement -100.5 to +12.3 ml), and sensitivity for heavy menstrual bleeding (>80 ml) was 47.1%. Choosing the picture closest to each pad's alkaline hematin volume would have produced a shortfall equal to 58% of the raters' shortfall, and the users' in-hand scores were also low (mean bias -38.2 ml). Krippendorff's alpha was 0.86 (95% CI 0.82-0.89) and the test-retest intraclass correlation 0.90, but in absolute terms raters' estimates of the same cycle had a pooled between-rater SD of 18.4 ml (up to 32.1 ml for a single cycle); among the 44 raters who repeated the task, the within-rater SD was 10.7 ml, and 6% of classifications changed on retest. LIMITATIONS, REASONS FOR CAUTION: A limited number of cycles were chosen from the original study to represent different cycle volumes; had other cycles been chosen, the results might have been better or worse. All pads were of one brand, only two cycles were not heavy, and raters scored photographs rather than handling pads. WIDER IMPLICATIONS OF THE FINDINGS: With the pictogram evaluated here, scoring of pad photographs systematically underestimated blood loss, partly because of the chart's fixed picture volumes, and estimates of the same cycle differed by tens of millilitres between raters and between sessions. High agreement statistics should not be taken as evidence that a chart accurately identifies blood loss above 80 ml per cycle. STUDY FUNDING/COMPETING INTEREST(S): This study was funded by the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development of the National Institutes of Health (NIH grant R44HD102235-03, awarded to TheraNova). A.Aw. and D.B. are co-founders of Quantiflow, which develops image-based methods for measuring menstrual blood loss, including the algorithm evaluated in the source study of the photographs used here. Quantiflow currently operates as a project of TheraNova, which holds the NIH grant that funded this study. Quantiflow is expected to be incorporated as an independent company in which A.Aw. and D.B. will hold equity. A.Aw. and D.B. have been compensated by TheraNova within the past 36 months. D.B. is a named inventor on a pending patent application related to Quantiflow's image-analysis algorithm. All other authors declare no competing interests. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: N/A.

papers.title: Determinants Of Knowledge And Awareness Of Obstetric Danger Signs Among Pregnant Women In Kumasi, Ghana: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: Background: Timely recognition of obstetric danger signs during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period is critical for reducing maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. In Ghana, maternal mortality remains high despite improvements in healthcare, partly due to inadequate awareness of these signs. This study assessed the knowledge and awareness of obstetric danger signs among pregnant women attending antenatal care (ANC) at Kwadaso SDA Hospital. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 200 pregnant women aged 18 years and above, recruited through simple random sampling. Data were collected using structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire adapted from JHPIEGO, covering sociodemographic information, obstetric history, knowledge of danger signs in different pregnancy phases and awareness-related attitudes. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 21, with descriptive statistics, Chi-square tests, and logistic regression used to assess associations. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: The most recognized obstetric danger signs were severe vaginal bleeding (97% antepartum, 85% intrapartum, and 92% postpartum) and retained placenta (95% intrapartum). Knowledge was high during the antepartum (86.5%) and intrapartum (78%) periods but dropped to 41% postpartum, resulting in 59% having poor overall knowledge. Women with 1to 3 children [(aOR=3.86, 95% CI: 1.31 to 11.36; p=0.014)] and 4 to 6 children [(aOR=6.12, 95% CI: 1.43 to 26.16; p=0.015)] were more likely to have good knowledge. Those with pregnancy-induced hypertension [(aOR=13.25, 95% CI: 1.10 to159.02; p=0.042)] and women who attended six to nine ANC visits [(aOR=8.98, 95% CI: 1.44 to 56.12; p=0.019)] also demonstrated increased likelihood of good knowledge, while participants with only primary education had lower odds [(aOR=0.06, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.46; p=0.007)]. Conclusion: Although awareness of some key obstetric danger signs, particularly bleeding, was high, overall knowledge remained inadequate, especially in the postpartum period. Strengthening targeted ANC education, with emphasis on postpartum complications, is essential to improve timely care-seeking and maternal outcomes in this population.

papers.title: Pregnancies complicated by high maternal BMI and placental inflammation have lower placental efficiency and infant Apgar scores at preterm
papers.abstract: Inflammation in pregnancy may elicit adverse pregnancy and newborn health outcomes. Obesity and chorioamnionitis are two prevalent conditions that can contribute to a pro-inflammatory environment in pregnancy. However, whether high placental inflammation identifies pregnancies complicated by maternal overweight/obesity or chorioamnionitis that are at greater risk of adverse outcomes, particularly in the absence of other major maternal comorbidities, remains unclear. Our primary objective was to examine whether high placental inflammation was associated with adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes in pregnancies complicated by maternal overweight/obesity or chorioamnionitis, in the absence of other major maternal comorbidities. Clinical data and placentae were obtained from 78 pregnancies across maternal prepregnancy BMI groups that delivered preterm (with and without chorioamnionitis) or term, without other major maternal comorbidities. Placental cytokine and chemokine protein expression levels were assessed by Bio-Plex immunoassay, and a pro-inflammatory summary score was derived. Placental samples with pro-inflammatory summary scores in the highest tertile were defined as having high placental inflammation, and samples with scores in the bottom two tertiles as without high inflammation. We assessed the combined effects of maternal overweight/obesity and high placental inflammation, and chorioamnionitis and high placental inflammation, on pregnancy, placental, and infant outcomes, comparing outcomes to overweight/obesity or chorioamnionitis affected pregnancies without high placental inflammation. Pregnancies complicated by maternal overweight/obesity and high placental inflammation had decreased birthweight-to-placental weight ratio (p=0.003) and lower infant Apgar scores (1-minute: p=0.03; 5-minute: p=0.01), compared to pregnancies with overweight/obesity without high placental inflammation, in preterm pregnancies only. In contrast, high placental inflammation among pregnancies with normal BMI did not associate with poorer outcomes. Chorioamnionitis cases with high placental inflammation also did not have poorer placental or infant outcomes compared to chorioamnionitis cases without high placental inflammation. Among pregnancies complicated by maternal overweight/obesity but no other major comorbidities, those with inflamed placentae may be most at risk for poor birth outcomes, particularly at preterm. Understanding placental phenotypes among sub-groups at greatest risk of adversity may allow for more targeted surveillance, early intervention, and individualised prenatal care.

papers.title: Maternal gut microbiome-metabolome signatures implicate vitamin B12 insufficiency and one-carbon dysregulation in fetal spina bifida despite folate repletion
papers.abstract: Despite folic acid fortification, neural tube defects (NTDs), including spina bifida, persist, suggesting contributing factors beyond folate status. The maternal gut microbiome influences the availability of nutrients and metabolites essential for neural tube closure and fetal development, yet its role in NTDs and associated comorbidities remains unclear. We investigated and integrated data from maternal gut microbial and circulating metabolic profiles in pregnancies affected by fetal spina bifida (cases) and unaffected pregnancies (controls) using shotgun metagenomics and targeted metabolomics. Despite comparable folate status, cases had lower serum vitamin B12 and enriched microbial cobalamin biosynthesis genes, suggesting disrupted B12 metabolism. Lower serum vitamin E, elevated amino acids, and altered antioxidant pathways indicated altered oxidative stress-related metabolism. Reduced microbial pyrimidine degradation and circulating purine metabolism suggested disrupted nucleotide metabolism. These findings implicate vitamin B12 insufficiency, a pro-oxidative environment, and altered nucleotide metabolism as potential pathways contributing to pathophysiology of NTDs and their comorbidities.

papers.title: Rethink the Flow: Establishing a Preanalytical Workflow for Protein Detection in Menstrual Effluent.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDMenstrual effluent (ME) is a promising, minimally invasive biofluid that contains unique protein biomarkers indicative of systemic and gynecological health. Despite its potential, the adoption of ME as a biofluid for disease identification remains limited because no standardized protocols exist for sample collection, processing, and storage. The lack of standardization remains a major challenge in ME research, introducing non-biological variability that limits accurate protein measurements and downstream interpretation for disease diagnosis. We examine how preanalytical factors, including centrifugation, freeze-thaw cycling, and pre-processing storage conditions, affect sample stability and protein concentration measurements. METHODSSingle-molecule array (Simoa) technology was used to quantify cancer antigen 125 (CA125) in ME samples collected from 19 participants. RESULTSWe found that delays in sample processing beyond eight hours increased the probability of unsuccessful fractionation (p < 0.02), a metric of sample stability. We detected CA125 in 100% of ME and ME-derived plasma samples; however, plasma showed better reproducibility across aliquots. Repeated freeze-thaw cycling significantly altered CA125 concentrations in plasma samples. ME samples stored at 4{degrees}C before centrifugation maintained their ability to fractionate and protein integrity for up to 120 hours. We also demonstrate that the developed workflow is compatible with longitudinal monitoring of CA125 in ME over three consecutive cycles. CONCLUSIONSThese results support at-home self-collection of ME for sample acquisition. Furthermore, the developed workflow enabled reliable protein biomarker analysis, facilitating the use of ME as a biofluid for biomarker discovery for gynecological diseases.

papers.title: Beyond billing codes: a proof-of-concept study of large language models for pregnancy episode reconstruction from clinical notes
papers.abstract: BackgroundAccurate identification of pregnancy episodes from electronic health records (EHRs) is essential for maternal and fetal health research. Existing approaches rely primarily on diagnosis and procedure codes, which may miss pregnancies documented outside the health system and are susceptible to coding errors. Clinical notes contain richer information but remain largely unexplored for this task. ObjectivesTo evaluate whether a large language model (LLM) can reconstruct complete pregnancy episodes directly from clinical notes. MethodsChronologically concatenated notes and messages were provided to GPT-5, which identified episodes and extracted variables including assisted reproductive treatment, gestational age, outcome, and complications. Performance was benchmarked against manual chart review (gold standard) and a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm in 30 patients comprising 74 pregnancies (20 patients in a held-out test set). ResultsThe LLM identified 53 of 54 test-set pregnancies versus 40/54 for a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm, with fewer spurious episodes (3 vs 24), corresponding to an F1 score for pregnancy detection against chart review of 0.96 vs 0.68. Among pregnancies identified by both methods, median absolute error was 0 vs 25.5 days for start dates (p<0.001) and 0 vs 1 day for end dates (p=0.044), and outcome accuracy was numerically but not significantly higher (0.84 vs 0.74 for exact outcome types; 0.92 vs 0.84 with abortion subtypes grouped). It additionally recovered information unavailable in structured data, including reproductive-treatment type and fetus-level outcomes. ConclusionsAn LLM applied to clinical narratives identified pregnancy episodes more completely and with more accurate dates than an ICD-code algorithm while capturing richer clinical detail. Because the two approaches used different input data, these gains reflect both the information in clinical notes and the LLM itself. LLM-based extraction from clinical notes is a promising complement to code-based pregnancy phenotyping that warrants evaluation in larger, multi-institutional cohorts.

papers.title: Risk mitigation and health communication: women's experiences and preferences in pregnancies with high body mass index.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAn increasing number of women in the UK enter into pregnancy with high BMI (BMI [≥]30kg/m2). On a population level, higher BMI is associated with an increased risk of pregnancy complications. However, many women experience communication from healthcare professionals about BMI-related risk as unsatisfactory. We aimed to explore how these dicussions could be made more acceptable by understanding how pregnant women with high BMI perceive, experience, and receive communication about their health and risk mitigation. MethodsWe recruited women with a booking BMI [≥]30kg/m2 from an antenatal ward at a tertiary maternity unit in the UK. Individual interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed. Data was analysed according to practical thematic analysis using qualitative analysis software. ResultsOur analysis (n=15 participants) revealed that BMI-related risk discourse resulted in a range of negative emotions, which aligned to four major themes: (i) BMI is unhelpful as a metric of health, (ii) healthy pregnancy is not determined by BMI, (iii) BMI-related risk is emotionally burdensome, and (iv) desire to personalise BMI-related risk. Pregnant women with high BMI did not perceive themselves or their pregnancies as unhealthy and did not necessarily desire additional support or investigations in pregnancy. Women reported that maternity staff emphasised BMI-related risk but gave little information on (i) what risk means for the individual, (ii) how to reduce BMI-related risk, and (iii) why interventions are offered, and (iv) how they can be declined. ConclusionRisk mitigation and health communication may be more acceptable to pregnant women with high BMI when it acknowledges the uncertainties and limitations of BMI, prioritises outcomes and gives information that matters to women with high BMI, and avoids weight-related stigma.

papers.title: Caesarean delivery patterns and selected maternal-neonatal outcomes in an urban Tanzanian referral hospital: a retrospective record review.
papers.abstract: BackgroundCaesarean delivery can be lifesaving when clinically indicated, but high facility rates require regular audit to distinguish appropriate emergency obstetric care from potentially avoidable operative delivery. This study described caesarean delivery patterns and selected maternal-neonatal outcomes among women delivering at Mwananyamala Regional Referral Hospital in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. MethodsA retrospective record review was conducted using complete delivery records from January 2025 to June 2025. The analytic dataset included 302 eligible records abstracted from delivery registers, admission records, and neonatal logs. The primary outcome was caesarean delivery. Associations were assessed using logistic regression restricted to variables available before or at the time of delivery decision. Post-delivery variables were not treated as predictors of caesarean delivery. Gestational-age values below 28 weeks or missing values were treated as invalid/missing and excluded from the study. ResultsMean maternal age was 28.09 {+/-} 6.68 years; 9.93% were <20 years, 68.87% were 20-34 years and 21.19% were [≥]35 years. Most women were multiparous (53.3%) and 43.71% delivered by caesarean section. In multivariable analysis, caesarean delivery was associated with employment (AOR=3.54; P<0.001), primigravity (AOR=2.65; P=0.009), prior uterine scar (AOR=1.89; P=0.002), and high-risk pregnancies (AOR=2.68; P=0.003). Maternal complications were infrequent, but postpartum hemorrhage was more common among older mothers. Neonatal outcomes were largely favorable, with 92.4% live births and 15.2% low birth weight. ConclusionCaesarean delivery was common among complete records at this urban referral hospital, but maternal age was not an independent predictor. The results support routine caesarean- delivery audit, improved delivery-register documentation, and future Robson-classification analysis once the necessary variables are captured reliably. What is already known -Maternal age, parity, high-risk pregnancy, previous caesarean delivery, and gestational age influence obstetric and neonatal outcomes. Facility-level caesarean delivery rates are increasingly used as markers of obstetric service utilization and quality, but crude rates are difficult to interpret without structured audit and adequate routine-data quality. What this study adds - This study found a high caesarean delivery rate (43.7%) and identified primigravity, prior uterine scar, and maternal comorbidities as predictors of caesarean delivery. Older maternal age was associated with increased postpartum hemorrhage, while stillbirth remained an important neonatal concern. The findings provide recent hospital-based evidence from an urban Tanzanian setting. How this study might affect research, practice or policy - The findings highlight the need for improved intrapartum monitoring, targeted management of high-risk pregnancies, and regular audits of caesarean delivery indications. Mwananyamala Regional Referral Hospital should strengthen delivery-register completeness, capture valid previous caesarean history for all women, and add missing variables needed for Robson Ten-Group Classification, especially fetal presentation or lie and number of fetus(es). The study also provides baseline data for future maternal health research.

papers.title: High-risk human papillomavirus detection across the cervical disease spectrum in Abuja, Nigeria: a comparative cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Cervical cancer remains a major public health problem in Nigeria, but data on high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) across the cervical disease spectrum are scarce for Abuja. We conducted a hospital-based comparative cross-sectional study of 101 women aged 25 years or older at Federal Medical Centre, Abuja: 59 with negative cytology (NILM) and 42 with cervical lesions (23 low- grade squamous intraepithelial lesions [LSIL], 8 high-grade lesions [HSIL], and 11 invasive cancers). Cervical specimens were tested using the Atila ScreenFire assay, which reports four pooled hrHPV target groups. hrHPV DNA was detected in 37/101 women (36.6%): 30.5% (18/59) in NILM, 26.1% (6/23) in LSIL, 50.0% (4/8) in HSIL, and 81.8% (9/11) in invasive cancer (Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact p = 0.005). Compared with NILM, invasive cancer had approximately tenfold higher odds of hrHPV detection (unadjusted odds ratio [OR] 10.25, 95% CI 2.01-52.28; age-adjusted OR 9.90, 95% CI 1.87-52.38). The HPV31/33/35/52/58 target group was detected most often (12.9%), followed by HPV16 and HPV18/45 (10.9% each) and HPV39/51/56/59/68 (5.9%). HPV16 was the most frequent target in invasive cancer (5/11). No target group was independently associated with lesion status. The NILM and lesion groups differed substantially in ethnicity, religion, and previous cervical screening, indicating different referral and screening pathways; the NILM group was not population-based. These findings show marked hrHPV enrichment in invasive cancer and substantial detection of non-16/18 target groups. They support HPV-based screening, genotype surveillance, and larger multicenter studies with population-based comparison groups.

papers.title: Beyond spouses: primary social supporter selection among pregnant women enrolled in the Support-Moms study in southwestern Uganda - a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Social support during pregnancy can influence womens engagement with antenatal care and other maternal health behaviours. Maternal health programmes in sub-Saharan Africa have often emphasised male partner involvement, although women may draw on broader social networks. Evidence on whom women identify as their primary supporter during pregnancy remains limited. We examined the prevalence and factors associated with non-spousal primary supporter selection among pregnant women in southwestern Uganda. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from the Support-Moms study, a Type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation randomised controlled trial conducted in Mbarara City, Mbarara District, and Mitooma District, southwestern Uganda. Pregnant women enrolled between 27 February and 17 December 2024 identified two social supporters before randomisation; the first-nominated individual was classified as the primary supporter. The primary outcome was selection of a non-spousal primary supporter. Modified Poisson regression with robust variance was used to estimate crude and adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Among 824 women, 223 (27.1%; 95% CI 24.1-30.3) selected a non-spousal primary supporter. Friends (30.5%) and other relatives (28.7%) were the most frequently nominated non-spousal supporters, followed by siblings (17.9%) and mothers (16.6%). Non-spousal selection was more prevalent among women recruited in Mbarara District (aPR 1.50, 95% CI 1.09-2.08) and Mitooma District (aPR 2.52, 95% CI 1.77-3.60) than Mbarara City, and among women who were separated, divorced, widowed, or never married (aPR 2.35, 95% CI 1.76-3.14), had an unplanned pregnancy (aPR 1.39, 95% CI 1.10-1.77), had a >10-year relationship with their nominated supporter (aPR 1.93, 95% CI 1.39-2.69), or were aged <20 years (aPR 1.48, 95% CI 1.01-2.15). Although spouses were the primary supporters for most women, more than one-quarter nominated someone else, most commonly a friend or relative. These findings suggest that pregnancy support extends beyond marital relationships and may be shaped by relational status, social context, pregnancy intention, age, and established social ties. Antenatal care programmes may benefit from complementing partner-focused approaches with mechanisms to engage other support figures identified by women.

papers.title: Maternal genetic risk for high body mass index and reduced infant mid-childhood educational attainment
papers.abstract: BackgroundMaternal body mass index (BMI) [≥]30kg/m2 has previously been associated with reduced infant neurocognitive development, including educational attainment. The mechanistic pathway underlying this association is unclear ObjectiveWe examined the relationship between observed maternal BMI, maternal genetic liability for BMI, and infant mid-childhood educational attainment. We aimed to limit residual confounding by environmental factors, for example socioeconomic status. MethodsA BMI polygenic risk score (PRSBMI) was applied to eligible participants in the Pregnancy Outcome Prediction study (n=2437). Six educational outcomes through mid-childhood (age 5, age 6, and 4 domains at age 7) were regressed on (i) maternal pre-pregnancy BMI based on self-reported weight (ii) maternal PRSBMI and (iii) residual BMI unexplained by PRSBMI. Participants were stratified into four risk groups by PRSBMI risk and observed BMI. Relationships between each risk group and educational outcomes were examined. All association analyses were adjusted for confounders including school funding type, socioeconomic status, and serious childhood morbidity. Causality was evaluated using two-sample Mendelian randomisation (MR). False discovery rate (FDR) was controlled using the Benjamini-Hochsberg correction at alpha=0.05. FindingsInverse associations were present between all education outcomes and maternal pre-pregnancy BMI, maternal PRSBMI, and maternal residual BMI. Children whose mothers had both pre-pregnancy BMI >25kg/m2 and PRSBMI z-score >0 were consistently less likely to meet educational standards compared to other risk groups. In two-sample MR an inverse relationship between maternal BMI and educational attainment was statistically significant for educational attainment aged 6, but not at ages 5 or 7 after FDR correction. InterpretationIncreased maternal pre-pregnancy BMI shows both genetic and environmental associations with reduced childhood educational attainment, although the two pathways are unlikely to be discrete. Infants of women with co-occurring high observed BMI and high genetic liability to BMI may be at highest risk of poor educational attainment.

papers.title: Hidden Dependencies in Endometriosis Microarray Classifiers: Sample Reuse, Outcome-Informed Batch Correction, and Diagnostic Reassessment
papers.abstract: Distinct Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) accessions do not necessarily represent independent transcriptomic samples. We investigated exact array reuse, access to test diagnoses during batch correction, and cohort and acquisition-date confounding in endometriosis classifiers. We compared decompressed CEL files using SHA-256, reconstructed a matrisome elastic-net workflow, changed test labels supplied to ComBat, and conducted 3,582 constrained training-label refits. We also evaluated the effect of removing matching training copies in a five-gene Huang-inspired random forest and performed a 324-probe nested internal benchmark within GSE51981. Of 37 test CEL files, 26 (70.3%) were identical to training arrays; all had been scanned in 2004-2005. Changing a test diagnosis supplied to ComBat moved the fixed classifier score toward the supplied label in all 37 interventions. In a deduplicated, batch-constrained comparison, median nominal balanced accuracy was 0.881 when ComBat received true test outcomes and 0.549 without them; the outcome-informed arm performed better in 1,193 of 1,194 matched refit comparisons. In the separate Huang-inspired reconstruction, removing each targets matching training copy lowered pooled AUC from 1.000 to 0.323 (conditional 95% interval 0.105-0.571). Exploratory nested AUC was 0.733 for endometriosis versus other gynecological conditions, and date-held-out AUC in 2009 was 0.698. For endometriosis versus healthy controls, a date-only out-of-fold model achieved AUC 0.935, compared with 0.893 for the molecular model. Together, these findings show how exact array reuse, outcome-informed preprocessing, and acquisition-date structure can compromise the interpretation of nominally independent validation. They describe reconstructions and exploratory internal analyses, not corrected performance estimates for the published classifiers.

papers.title: Prenatal care and clinical characteristics of adolescent pregnancies
papers.abstract: BackgroundDescriptions of adolescent pregnancy can identify priorities for prenatal care and postpartum follow-up. This study characterized prenatal care and clinical outcomes documented in adolescent pregnancy records. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective, descriptive, observational cross-sectional review of records covering 2020-2024 at a single family medicine outpatient service. All eligible records were included. Prenatal care and clinical characteristics were summarized using frequencies and percentages. Reporting was restricted to aggregate results to reduce the risk of participant identification. ResultsThirty-nine records were analyzed. The first prenatal visit occurred in the second trimester in 53.85%. Overweight or obesity was recorded in 71.8%. Urinary tract infection occurred in 66.67% and gestational hypertension in 28.21%. No preterm births or obstetric hemorrhages were recorded. Vaginal delivery accounted for 51.28% and cesarean delivery for 48.72%. Postpartum contraceptive method was unspecified in 64.10% of records. ConclusionsThis small, single-center study identified frequent urinary tract infections, a high recorded proportion of overweight or obesity, prenatal entry commonly after the first trimester, and incomplete postpartum contraceptive documentation. These findings identify local priorities for care and record quality; they do not establish causal relationships or population prevalence.

papers.title: Beyond prescription: Determinants of low-dose aspirin adoption and uptake across the pre-eclampsia prevention pathway in Nepal - a qualitative study guided by the COM-B model
papers.abstract: Despite strong evidence supporting low-dose aspirin (LDA) for preventing pre-eclampsia among women at risk, implementation remains suboptimal globally. The prevention pathway encompasses early antenatal care engagement, screening and risk identification, prescribing LDA, and medication uptake. This qualitative study explored barriers and facilitators to LDA adoption by providers (i.e., prescribing) and uptake among women in Nepal. A qualitative study was conducted with pregnant women, healthcare providers, and maternal and child health stakeholders in Nepal. Data collection and analysis were guided by the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation, and Behavior (COM-B) model. Participants were purposively recruited from three tertiary hospitals and maternal health organizations. Semi-structured interviews explored experiences and perspectives related to antenatal care, such as pre-eclampsia risk screening, LDA prescribing, and uptake. Data were analyzed using rapid qualitative analysis and organized according to the COM-B components. Seventy-three participants were interviewed, including 36 pregnant women, both at risk and not at risk for pre-eclampsia; 29 healthcare providers, including consultant/senior obstetricians, mid-level doctors, and nurses or midwives; and 8 maternal and child health stakeholders representing government, multi-lateral, non-governmental, professional, and academic institutions. LDA adoption and uptake were affected by interdependent gaps across the prevention pathway. Delayed antenatal care engagement and inconsistent screening limited timely identification of women at risk, while gaps in national guidance and standardized prescribing protocols contributed to variable provider prescribing practices. Among women prescribed LDA, clear counselling on its purpose and safety and trust in providers supported uptake. LDA adoption and uptake depend on a functioning prevention pathway in which women engage with antenatal care early enough for timely risk assessment, those at risk are identified through screening, providers prescribe appropriately, and women are supported to use the medication. Strengthening this pathway requires coordinated attention to health-system and provider capacity as well as communication with women, rather than strategies focused narrowly on prescribing or medication use. These findings will inform the development of implementation strategies for Nepal and other low-resource settings seeking to integrate evidence-based preventive interventions into maternal healthcare systems.

papers.title: Adrenergic nerve fibers are depleted in adenomyosis myometrium
papers.abstract: Structured AbstractO_ST_ABSObjectiveC_ST_ABSUterine dyscontractility in adenomyosis and endometriosis is at the heart of pain symptoms and disease pathogenesis. To elucidate possible causes of dyscontractility, we examined the distribution of smooth muscle, blood vessel, collagen and nerve fibers in full-thickness, serosa-to-endometrium myometrium of adenomyosis patients versus control. DesignRetrospective study. SubjectsUterine biopsies from patients who underwent hysterectomy for adenomyosis (n = 26) or other non-adenomyosis indications (n=22, mostly myomas). Main Outcome MeasuresDensity profiles along the serosa-to-endometrium axis of smooth muscle (SMA), endothelium (PECAM), general innervation (PGP9.5) and adrenergic innervation (TH) obtained by immunofluorescence, mosaic epifluorescence imaging and machine-learning assisted segmentation. Fibrous collagen type I&III was quantified by second-harmonic generation microscopy (SHG). ResultsThe density profiles of smooth muscle, endothelium, collagen and PGP9.5 were similar between both patient groups. Sympathetic adrenergic nerve fiber density radiated from the serosa inwards, with a continuously decreasing density from the outer to the inner myometrium. Adrenergic inhibitory nerve fibers were 4 times less dense in the inner myometrium of adenomyosis uteri compared to controls. ConclusionThe enrichment of inhibitory adrenergic nerve fibers in the outer vs inner myometrium provides a neuro-muscular mechanism by which contractions are restricted to the inner myometrium outside of pregnancy. The depletion of TH fibers in adenomyosis implies that a higher thickness of myometrium is involved in uterine contractions, thus explaining junctional zone thickening and dyscontractility in this pathology. This depletion may be due to defective post-pregnancy adrenergic re-innervation of the myometrium.

papers.title: Perioperative Safety, Surgical Morbidity, and Survival Outcomes of Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy (NACT-IDS) versus Primary Debulking Surgery (PDS) in Elderly Patients with Advanced Epithelial Ovarian Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundAdvanced epithelial ovarian cancer disproportionately affects older women. While primary debulking surgery (PDS) is the traditional gold standard, it carries substantial morbidity and mortality risks in frail, older patients. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval debulking surgery (NACT-IDS) can downstage disease and mitigate these surgical risks, but high-level evidence syntheses specific to geriatric populations remain limited. MethodsThis systematic review and meta-analysis adhered to PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261461644). Five electronic databases and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for comparative studies evaluating NACT-IDS versus PDS in women aged 70 years (or 65 years in defined geriatric cohorts) with FIGO Stage IIIC/IV epithelial ovarian cancer. Outcomes were synthesized using random-effects models. Methodological quality was assessed via the ROBINS-I tool, cumulative evidence reliability via Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA), and overall evidence certainty via the GRADE framework. ResultsEleven retrospective cohort studies encompassing over 16,500 older patients met the inclusion criteria. NACT-IDS yielded an 80% reduction in unadjusted 30-day perioperative mortality compared to PDS (RR = 0.20, 95% CI [0.05, 0.89], p = 0.034). Furthermore, NACT-IDS significantly decreased hospital length of stay (MD = -3.12 days, p = 0.0044) and increased the likelihood of complete macroscopic resection (R0 = 0 cm) by 74% (RR = 1.74, 95% CI [1.01, 3.02], p = 0.047). Severe complications (Clavien-Dindo 3) trended lower with NACT-IDS (RR = 0.38, 95% CI [0.13, 1.08]). Unadjusted overall survival models demonstrated a 13% increased hazard of death for NACT-IDS (HR = 1.13, 95% CI [1.04, 1.23]); however, this primarily reflects profound selection bias (confounding by indication) where the frailest patients were systematically triaged to the NACT-IDS pathway. The overall certainty of evidence was appraised as Very Low. ConclusionFor older women with advanced epithelial ovarian cancer, NACT-IDS significantly improves perioperative safety, accelerates hospital recovery, and maximizes complete resection rates compared to upfront PDS. While retrospective survival data are heavily skewed by channeling bias, NACT-IDS effectively protects physiological reserve and should be strongly considered as the standard initial management strategy for this vulnerable demographic.

papers.title: Decision for hysterectomy as a modifiable cardiovascular risk factor: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo describe the role of hysterectomy in modifying the major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Data sourcesPubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and ScienceDirect were searched from database inception to March 10, 2026. Study eligibility criteriaFull-text randomized controlled trials, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, case series, and experimental studies reporting new-onset cardiovascular events, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, or other metabolic effects following hysterectomy were eligible. Reviews and book chapters were excluded. Study appraisal and synthesis methodsStudy selection and data extraction were performed independently by multiple reviewers with conflicts resolved by consensus. Cohort study quality was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; a modified version assessed cross-sectional studies. Meta-analyses were performed using a generic inverse-variance random-effects model for each outcome, stratified by study design (cross-sectional versus cohort) and effect measure (adjusted odds ratio, adjusted hazard ratio, or relative risk). Narrative synthesis was performed for outcomes not meeting criteria for meta-analysis. ResultsTwenty studies (11 cohort, 8 cross-sectional, 1 mixed design) were included after screening 18,337 records from four databases. Hysterectomy was associated with significantly increased risk of hypertension (cross-sectional odds ratio 1.32, 95% confidence interval 1.18- 1.48; cohort hazard ratio 1.19, 95% confidence interval 1.09-1.30), diabetes (cross-sectional odds ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.11-1.32; cohort hazard ratio 1.20, 95% confidence interval 1.13-1.29), hyperlipidemia (hazard ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.13-1.29), obesity (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.03-1.50), and metabolic syndrome (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.08-1.44). ConclusionsHysterectomy is associated with increased risk of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and metabolic syndrome, key modifiable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Active cardiovascular risk assessment and follow-up may be warranted for women who undergo hysterectomy, particularly at a young age.

papers.title: Communication without dialogue? Framing patient-professional interaction in UK institutional discourse on pregnancy loss
papers.abstract: Communication failures are repeatedly implicated in harmful experiences and outcomes in pregnancy care, especially in contexts of loss, yet little is known about how communication itself is represented in the institutional texts that shape expectations of care. This study examines the extent to which communication is discussed, and how patient-healthcare professional interaction is framed, in publicly accessible UK discourse about pregnancy loss. Two corpora comprising texts from seven medical organisations (120,383 words) and eight charities (224,481 words) were divided into healthcare professional-facing and patient-facing sub-corpora. Frequency, semantic keyness, keyword and concordance analyses were conducted using Wmatrix7. In medical discourse, language and communicative interaction were underrepresented, while speech acts associated with unidirectional professional activities such as advising, recommending and referring were overrepresented. Compared with charity texts, medical outputs foregrounded clinical evidence, policy, risk and professional knowledge. Characteristic forms including "confirmed", "advised", "recommended" and "offered" frequently occurred in passive or agentless constructions that positioned patients principally as recipients of information; patient agency was most visible in "reporting" symptoms or concerns. Charity discourse more often foregrounded talking, listening, feelings, preferences, wording, lived experience, and patient knowledge; representing communication as active and bidirectional. We argue that UK medical discourse constructs communication primarily as the transmission of authorised knowledge rather than as relational clinical practice, reinforcing a paternalistic distribution of communicative agency. Medical institutions should embed listening, reciprocal dialogue, sensitivity to language preferences, and checks on understanding as core standards of safe pregnancy care.

papers.title: Associations Between Cannabis Use and Sleep Outcomes in a Sample of Pregnant Women
papers.abstract: ImportanceBoth sleep difficulties and cannabis use during pregnancy (CUP) are common and associated with adverse birth and offspring outcomes. Sleep problems are a commonly reported motive for cannabis use during pregnancy. ObjectiveEstimate associations between cannabis use during pregnancy and common sleep difficulties across trimesters. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsThis cohort study recruited pregnant women with lifetime cannabis use who used (n=298) and did not use (n=143) cannabis during pregnancy. Women who reported heavy episodic alcohol consumption or use of other illicit substances were excluded. Some women tested positive for cotinine in urine drug screens. ExposuresCannabis use was assessed at each trimester using self-report and urine drug screening. Presence of the nicotine metabolite, cotinine, was measured via urine drug screening at each trimester. Cannabis use during pregnancy (CUP) status was defined separately for each trimester as use versus no use and was treated as a time-varying exposure. The nicotine metabolite cotinine was included as a covariate in all models to account for nicotine exposure. Motivation for cannabis use during pregnancy was assessed during the first trimester. Main Outcomes and MeasuresInsomnia symptoms (Womens Health Initiative Insomnia Rating Scale), daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale), subjective sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index single item), and restless legs symptoms were assessed at each trimester. ResultsA CUP Status x Trimester interaction was observed for insomnia symptoms (F(2,737.81)=4.98, PFDR=0.03) wherein use during the third trimester was associated with heightened insomnia. Women reporting sleep difficulties as a motive for use reported worse insomnia symptoms (F(1, 223)=13.09, PFDR=0.001) and worse sleep quality (F(1, 219)=7.86, PFDR=0.01), relative to those using for other reasons. ConclusionElevated third trimester insomnia symptoms among pregnant women using cannabis compared to women who did not use cannabis suggest a potential trimester-sensitive association. Despite perceptions that cannabis improves sleep, women who reported sleep as their motive for CUP during the first trimester experienced greater insomnia symptoms and poorer sleep quality across pregnancy than those using cannabis for other reasons. Additional studies are needed to determine whether sleep-related difficulties precede cannabis use, follow it, are modified by it, or represent an epiphenomenon. KEY POINTSO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSIs cannabis use during pregnancy associated with maternal sleep problems? FindingsWithin this study of 441 pregnant women, cannabis use was associated with higher third trimester insomnia symptoms but not with other sleep outcomes. Women using cannabis to aid with sleep difficulties had worse insomnia symptoms and poorer sleep quality than those using for other reasons. MeaningCannabis use in late pregnancy may mark periods of greater insomnia symptom burden, suggesting that sleep problems during pregnancy may be an important clinical context for understanding cannabis use during pregnancy.

papers.title: Placental Klotho responses to supervised prenatal exercise: findings from the PLACENTRAINING study
papers.abstract: BackgroundRegular exercise during pregnancy improves maternal and neonatal outcomes; however, the molecular pathways underlying placental adaptations to prenatal exercise remain poorly understood. Klotho is a cytoprotective protein involved in the regulation of oxidative stress, metabolic homeostasis, and cellular resilience, yet whether placental Klotho concentrations are associated with prenatal exercise has not been previously investigated. AimsThe primary aim of this study was to examine whether participation in a supervised concurrent exercise program during pregnancy is associated with placental Klotho concentrations at birth. Secondary aims were to explore potential fetal sex-specific patterns and associations between placental Klotho and selected biomarkers related to angiogenic and inflammatory pathways. MethodsPregnant women were allocated to either a supervised concurrent exercise program or usual care. The intervention comprised combined aerobic and resistance training performed three times per week from early-mid pregnancy until birth. Placental tissue was collected at birth, and Klotho concentrations were quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Secondary analyses explored potential sex-specific patterns and examined associations between placental Klotho, placental weight, and a panel of placental biomarkers. ResultsSeventy-six women were included (exercise: n = 41; control: n = 35). Placental Klotho concentrations were significantly higher in the exercise group, with an adjusted mean difference of approximately 101 pg/mL (p = 0.001; partial {superscript 2} = 0.164). This effect was consistent across fetal sex, with no significant exercise-by-sex interaction. Several placental biomarkers were independently associated with Klotho, suggesting a potential relationship with angiogenic and inflammatory signaling pathways. ConclusionsParticipation in a supervised concurrent exercise program during pregnancy is associated with higher placental Klotho concentrations at birth, irrespective of fetal sex. These findings provide novel insight into molecular pathways potentially involved in placental adaptations associated with prenatal exercise and reinforce the concept of the placenta as an exercise-responsive organ during pregnancy.

papers.title: Development and internal validation of early- and mid-pregnancy prediction models for macrosomia in nulliparous singleton pregnancies
authors: M. B. van der Hout-van der Jagt
papers.abstract: PurposeMacrosomia is associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes, but early risk stratification remains challenging. Most existing prediction approaches rely on later-pregnancy ultrasound measurements, limiting opportunities for earlier preventive counseling and monitoring. MethodsIn this secondary analysis of the prospective nuMoM2b cohort in the United States, we included 6,371 nulliparous singleton pregnancies selected for available periconceptional diet and ultrasound data at Visits 2 and 3. We developed visit-updated multivariable logistic regression models for birthweight >4000 g and >4500 g using routinely available maternal characteristics, anthropometry, periconceptional diet, and serial ultrasound measurements, with sensitivity analyses using large-for-gestational-age birthweight. Model performance was assessed by repeated stratified cross-validation and compared with World Health Organization fetal growth chart-based ultrasound percentile benchmarks, emphasizing the estimated fetal weight percentile as the most clinically familiar proxy. ResultsBirthweight >4000 g and >4500 g occurred in 7.9% and 1.2% of pregnancies, respectively. Models updated with later pregnancy information achieved the best discrimination, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.73 for birthweight >4000 g and 0.82 for birthweight >4500 g. In this selected analytic cohort, the early-pregnancy model based on maternal data alone provided moderate discrimination (0.63 and 0.72, respectively), although lower than the strongest third-trimester WHO fetal growth chart-based ultrasound percentile benchmarks. ConclusionWithin this selected cohort, routinely available early-pregnancy maternal characteristics and anthropometry provided moderate risk stratification for macrosomia, and later ultrasound measurements improved performance further. Estimates for birthweight >4500 g require caution given the 77 events. External validation is required before clinical implementation. What this study adds to the clinical workRoutinely available early-pregnancy maternal characteristics and anthropometry provided moderate risk stratification for macrosomia in nulliparous singleton pregnancies. Visit-updated models incorporating later ultrasound measurements improve discrimination further and may help refine surveillance during pregnancy.

papers.title: Contraceptive efficacy of 50 mg Mifepristone once-a-week: an open label, single-arm, multicenter clinical trial in Moldova
papers.abstract: IntroductionUnmet needs for contraception persist partly due to side effects, dissatisfaction, and medical contraindications. Mechanistic and clinical data support the contraceptive potential of mifepristone, which may provide a non-estrogen contraceptive option, but evidence remains limited. The primary aim of this trial was to evaluate the contraceptive efficacy and safety of once-weekly 50 mg mifepristone. MethodWe conducted an open-label, single-arm, multicenter trial in Moldova. Women aged 18-35 years used mifepristone as their sole contraceptive method for 13 cycles. The primary endpoint was pregnancy due to method failure, expressed as a Pearl Index (PI). ResultsOf 170 women enrolled between August 2023 and May 2025, 146 initiated treatment. Two pregnancies occurred during 1,187 evaluable cycles, with a perfect-use at-risk PI of 1.55 (95% CI, 0.04-8.64). Increased endometrial thickness occurred in 8.9% (11/123) of participants and progesterone receptor modulator-associated endometrial changes in 10.6% (13/123), which normalized at follow up. No hyperplasia or cellular atypia was detected in any of the endometrial biopsies. Bleeding averaged one day per cycle, and 60% reported no bleeding or spotting at treatment end. Overall, 95.6% were satisfied or very satisfied with the method. ConclusionsDue to early discontinuation of the trial the study did not achieve the planned sample size. The subsequent imprecise estimated PI did not meet the prespecified efficacy criterion. However, the favorable safety profile, bleeding pattern, and high acceptability supports continued development of mifepristone as a contraceptive. Key MessageEvidence for mifepristone as regular contraception remains limited. 50 mg once weekly showed high acceptability, reduced bleeding, and reversible endometrial changes, expanding evidence for its contraceptive development. The contraceptive efficacy of mifepristone requires confirmation in larger trials.

papers.title: Anticipating conversion to hysterectomy in women counseled for myomectomy: temporal validation of the EFFAH score at a Ghanaian district hospital
papers.abstract: BackgroundIn women with uterine fibroids counseled for myomectomy, consent typically involves discussing the preoperative probability that the surgery will end in hysterectomy. To our knowledge, no published tool estimates this probability, including in sub-Saharan Africa. This study aimed to temporally validate the Estimating Fibroid Factors Associated with Hysterectomy (EFFAH) score (an eight-item bedside score) in a later cohort at a district hospital in Ghana, to define risk groups for counseling and triage. MethodsIn this retrospective cohort study with temporal external validation, the development cohort comprised 392 records of women counseled for myomectomy with possible hysterectomy who underwent surgery at Catholic Hospital, Battor, in 2013 to 2014. A pilot analysis was conducted in July 2025 to arrive at the odds ratio used to calculate a validation sample size of 416. The validation cohort comprised 800 women counseled for myomectomy with possible hysterectomy in 2017 to 2019. The score assigns points to eight items from the history, abdominal examination, hemoglobin and renal ultrasound. We assessed discrimination, calibration and net benefit of the development equation with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), updated it by closed testing and compared it with AutoScore, a random forest-based points score. ResultsHysterectomy was performed in 31.6% of women in the development cohort and 21.1% in the validation cohort. The C-statistic was 0.76 (95% CI: 0.70, 0.80) at development and 0.73 (95% CI: 0.69, 0.77) at validation. The development equation overestimated risk, with an observed-to-expected ratio of 0.69 (95% CI: 0.60, 0.78) and a calibration slope of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.63, 1.03), and an intercept-only update was selected. The observed proportion with hysterectomy was 6.2% for scores of 0 to 2, 23.5% for 3 to 4 and 42.2% for [≥]5; a score below 3 yielded a negative predictive value of 93.8% (95% CI: 90.1, 96.2). AutoScore yielded a C-statistic of 0.74 (95% CI: 0.69, 0.78) and did not outperform the score (difference 0.01; 95% CI: -0.02, 0.04). ConclusionsThe EFFAH score ranked women by their risk of hysterectomy in a later cohort at the same hospital, and an intercept update aligned its average predicted risk with the observed proportion in that cohort. Clinically, about 6 in 100 women scoring 0 to 2 and about 4 in 10 women scoring [≥]5 underwent hysterectomy; for the latter, explicit consent for hysterectomy, a senior surgeon and readily available cross-matched blood are proposed. Because it uses only routine preoperative findings, the score could support consent and resource planning in resource-limited and resource-rich settings alike, after local recalibration and prospective multicenter evaluation.

papers.title: Maternal Vaginal Pathogenic Bacterial Colonization and Early-Onset Neonatal Sepsis in Mwanza City, Tanzania: A Prospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: BackgroundEarly-onset neonatal sepsis (EONS) remains a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries. Maternal vaginal pathogenic bacterial colonization and HIV infection may increase the risk of EONS through vertical transmission and immune dysregulation, but prospective evidence from sub-Saharan Africa is limited. This study assessed the association between maternal HIV status, vaginal pathogenic bacterial colonization, and EONS among women delivering at five selected health facilities in Mwanza City, Tanzania. MethodsA prospective comparative cohort study was conducted between August 2023 and February 2025 among 580 pregnant women delivering at five selected health facilities in Mwanza City. A maternal lower vaginal swab was collected before delivery for bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Neonates were followed for seven days after birth to identify EONS using standardized clinical and laboratory criteria, with culture confirmation where applicable. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression were used to estimate incidence rates and identify independent predictors of neonatal sepsis. ResultsOverall, 89 neonates developed EONS, yielding a cumulative incidence of 15.3% and an incidence rate of 2.42 per 100 person-days (95% CI: 1.97-2.98). Twenty-four (27.0%) cases were culture-confirmed, while 65 (73.0%) were clinically diagnosed. Neonates born to colonized mothers had substantially higher sepsis incidence than those born to non-colonized mothers (3.41 vs. 0.34 per 100 person-days). After adjustment, maternal vaginal bacterial colonization was the strongest predictor of neonatal sepsis (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 9.52, 95% CI: 3.47-26.09; p<0.001). Maternal HIV infection independently increased the hazard of neonatal sepsis by 76% (aHR 1.76, 95% CI: 1.14-2.73; p=0.011), while maternal malaria doubled the risk (aHR 2.74, 95% CI: 1.43-5.22; p=0.002). Escherichia coli (E. coli) accounted for 58.3% of culture-confirmed neonatal infections, followed by both Klebsiella pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus (20.8% each). ConclusionMaternal vaginal pathogenic bacterial colonization was strongly associated with early-onset neonatal sepsis. Maternal HIV infection and malaria were also independently associated with increased sepsis. The findings support strengthening maternal infection prevention, neonatal surveillance, and microbiological diagnostic capacity, while prospective intervention studies are needed to determine whether targeted screening and prevention of maternal bacterial colonization can reduce neonatal sepsis.

papers.title: Receipt of guideline-concordant prenatal care among Medicaid-insured women with disabilities in Texas
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo assess receipt of guideline-concordant prenatal care among pregnant women with disabilities enrolled in Medicaid. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of 748,304 births to women enrolled in Texas Medicaid from 2010-2015. Births were classified into three groups by maternal disability status: no disability, receipt of federal disability benefits (STAR+), or disability identified through ICD-9 codes. Guideline-concordant care was defined as receipt of recommended prenatal services at recommended times. Multivariable logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for guideline-concordant care, adjusting for covariates. ResultsThere were 20,700 births (2.8%) to women with disabilities, 40.1% of whom were enrolled in STAR+. Fewer than half of women in any group received guideline-concordant testing for D(Rh) antigen, rubella, complete blood count, bacteriuria, or glucose tolerance. Women in STAR+ were more likely than those without disabilities to receive no prenatal care (9.4% vs. 1.6%), despite higher first-trimester initiation among those who accessed care. STAR+ enrollment was associated with substantially lower odds of guideline-concordant testing, including HIV (aOR 0.27; 95% CI, 0.26-0.29), syphilis (0.33; 0.31-0.35), hepatitis B (0.38; 0.36-0.40), D(Rh) antigen (0.31; 0.30-0.33), anatomy ultrasound (0.32; 0.31-0.34), and glucose (0.42; 0.40-0.44). Women with disabilities identified via ICD-9 codes also had lower odds, though differences were smaller. Conclusion for practiceGuideline-concordant prenatal care was suboptimal overall and especially deficient among women receiving federal disability benefits, underscoring the need for targeted quality improvement in Medicaid prenatal care delivery. SignificanceO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this subject?C_ST_ABSPregnant women with disabilities face substantially higher risks of severe maternal morbidity, gestational complications, and adverse infant outcomes. Evaluating whether Medicaid delivers guideline-concordant prenatal care to this population is essential for identifying care gaps in a major safety-net program. What this study addsIn this cohort study, receipt of guideline-concordant prenatal care was low overall and significantly lower among women with disabilities. Women receiving federal disability benefits (STAR+) had the lowest concordance rates and were more likely to receive no prenatal care compared to women without disabilities.

papers.title: Update of the ADNEX risk model (ADNEX2) to diagnose ovarian cancer in surgically and conservatively managed patients with an adnexal mass: multicentre prospective cohort study
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThe ADNEX ultrasound-based prediction model estimates the probability that an adnexal mass is benign, borderline, stage I primary invasive, stage II-IV primary invasive, or secondary metastatic. ADNEX was developed on patients managed surgically. We aimed to update ADNEX to ADNEX2 using more recent data on both surgically and conservatively managed patients. ADNEX2 is designed for use in patients in whom the benign descriptors (BDs), a set of ultrasound profiles with an estimated risk of malignancy below 1%, do not apply. DesignSecondary analysis of a multicentre prospective cohort study. Setting17 oncology and non-oncology centres from 8 European countries. ParticipantsPatients with a newly detected adnexal mass recruited between 2012 and 2016 who were managed surgically or conservatively with clinical and ultrasound follow-up. InterventionsADNEX2 uses the same predictors as ADNEX (age, type of centre, lesion diameter, proportion of solid tissue, number of papillary projections, >10 cyst locules, ascites and acoustic shadows and CA125). Model updating involved logistic recalibration followed by Bayesian refitting. Validation was based on leave-one-centre-out cross-validation. ADNEX2 and ADNEX include CA125 but also work without CA125. Main outcome measuresModel performance regarding discrimination (AUC), calibration (plots and observed:expected, O:E, ratio), and clinical utility (net benefit). ResultsOf 6847 patients, 4625 (68%) had a benign tumour, 1710 (25%) had a malignant tumour, while tumour outcome was uncertain for 512 (7%) patients. BDs applied in 2190 (32%) patients, of whom 0.5% (95% CI, 0.2%-0.9%) had a malignancy. A two-step strategy using BDs followed by ADNEX2 had an AUC of 0.95 (0.94-0.96) to distinguish benign from malignant tumours. When evaluated on 4657 patients in whom BDs did not apply, ADNEX2 had an AUC of 0.93 (0.91-0.94). The two-step strategy with ADNEX2 was better calibrated than the two-step strategy with ADNEX (O:E ratio of 1.05 versus 1.14) and had marginally higher clinical utility. Not including available CA125 values in ADNEX2 reduced the ability to distinguish stage II-IV primary invasive tumours from other invasive malignancies. ConclusionsADNEX2 is better calibrated than ADNEX. CA125 measurement is not crucial to estimate the risk of malignancy, but is recommended to estimate the risk of malignant subtypes. Trial registration: clinicaltrials.gov NCT01698632. What is already known on this topic- The IOTA ADNEX risk model is widely used to estimate the probability that an adnexal mass is benign or one of four malignant subtypes, and has been integrated into a two-step strategy following the application of ultrasound benign descriptors (BDs). - Like nearly all prediction models for adnexal masses, the original ADNEX model was developed exclusively using data from patients who underwent surgery (recruited between 1999 and 2012). This introduces selection bias when the model is used to determine who should be referred for specialized care. - Measuring serum CA125 is not essential for estimating overall malignancy risk, but is recommended when patients are referred to oncology centres to distinguish stage II-IV primary invasive cancer from stage I primary invasive cancer and secondary metastases. What this study adds- ADNEX was updated to ADNEX2 using more recent multicentre data (IOTA5) including both surgically and conservatively managed patients with tumours to which benign descriptors did not apply. - ADNEX2 (used alone or in a two-step strategy after benign descriptors) maintains high discrimination (AUC 0.95 for two-step strategy with ADNEX2; 0.93 when benign descriptors do not apply), improves risk calibration compared with the original ADNEX model (O:E ratio 1.05 v 1.14), and offers marginally higher clinical utility.

papers.title: Caesarean section in Bangladesh, 2012-13 to 2025: facility birth, the private sector and small-area geography
papers.abstract: BackgroundIn Bangladesh, caesarean section rose from one in five births in 2012-13 to one in two in 2025. We asked how much of this rise came from more facility births, a move to private facilities, and changing rates within sectors. MethodsThis repeated cross-sectional study used Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys from 2012-13, 2019 and 2025 (26,539 recent mothers). A Kitagawa decomposition split the rise into parts. For 2025, we mapped caesarean use among facility births in 2,720 clusters and examined modelled travel time. ResultsThe caesarean rate rose from 19.5% (95% CI 18.1 to 20.9) to 52.0% (50.7 to 53.2). More facility births made up 82.8% (78.9 to 87.7) of this 32.5 point rise and the move to private facilities 12.6% (10.1 to 15.0). In a one-step version, place of birth made up 94.7% (90.7 to 98.9). The private caesarean rate rose from 79.1% to 86.1%, while the public rate fell from 38.7% to 33.5%. Among private first births, which rarely follow a previous caesarean, the 2025 rate was 4.8 points (0.3 to 10.2) above the 2012-13 models prediction. The 2025 private rate was 85% to 87% in every wealth group. Longer travel time was linked with fewer caesareans, mainly through fewer facility births. Among private-sector births, travel time was not linked with caesarean (prevalence ratio 0.99 per 10 minutes, 0.97 to 1.01). Caesarean use among facility births clustered geographically; the private share of births in nearby clusters, not household factors, accounted for much of this. ConclusionsIn accounting terms, most of the rise came from births moving into facilities, mostly private ones, where caesarean was already common. The data cannot show how many caesareans were needed. If 2025 sector mix and rates persist, more facility births would keep raising the national rate.

papers.title: A clinical audit of postoperative care after emergency caesarean section for obstructed labour at a national referral hospital in Uganda
papers.abstract: BackgroundPostoperative complications after emergency caesarean section (C/S) due to obstructed labour (O/L) are a significant contributing factor to maternal morbidity in low-resource settings. At Kawempe National Referral Hospital (KNRH) in Kampala, Uganda, hospital records from late 2024 showed an overall adverse outcome rate of approximately 10% among all women delivered by caesarean section, with postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) and surgical site infection (SSI) among the recorded outcomes. Women who deliver by C/S for O/L are particularly a high-risk group, yet adherence to postoperative care standards in this group had not been systematically evaluated. This audit therefore aimed at assessing whether a clinical audit could improve the quality of postoperative care among women undergoing C/S for O/L. MethodsA criterion-based audit cycle was conducted at a national referral hospital in Kampala, Uganda over six months. At baseline, 150 case files of mothers who delivered by caesarean section due to O/L were reviewed retrospectively, and care practices were evaluated against six care standards derived from World Health Organization (WHO) and Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) guidelines. These included: monitoring of vital signs (blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature, oxygen saturation), administration of analgesia, surgical site care, administration of prophylactic and empirical antibiotics, monitoring for postpartum haemorrhage (monitoring uterine tone and vaginal bleeding), and bladder care. Findings were shared with stakeholders, and gaps were identified. Interventions such as continuous medical education (CME) sessions, protocol dissemination, and workflow adjustments, co-developed with stakeholders, were rigorously implemented for 2 months and 2 weeks. An endline audit was done by reviewing 149 case files. Data analysis involved a comparative description of the baseline and endline audits to determine statistical significance using a chi-square test. To assess the overall level of adherence to postoperative care standards, a composite indicator overall mean care score was computed for both baseline and endline phases. This metric was derived by aggregating compliance across all evaluated components of the standards. ResultsStatistically significant improvements were noted in three standards: Antibiotic administration-prophylactic antibiotics administration (38.0% to 60.4%; p<0.001) and empiric antibiotics administration on Day 1(metronidazole-13.7% to 96.2%, p<0.001), urine output monitoring on Day 1(17.3% to 28.9%; p=0.012), and analgesia administration (paracetamol and rectal diclofenac-50% to above 80%, p<0.002). However, critical gaps persisted, with no observed improvement in vital sign monitoring and surgical site care, and a paradoxical decline in uterine tone monitoring (90.0 to 88.7%; p=0.667). The overall mean care score improved from 46.7% at baseline to 61.1% at endline (absolute increase of +14.4% points). ConclusionThe results of this study show that a clinical audit is a feasible quality improvement tool that can enhance postoperative care for mothers who deliver by C/S due to O/L in low-resource settings. However, there is a need to evaluate the other standards that did not have an improvement.

papers.title: Maternal epigenetic age acceleration in early pregnancy, gestational duration, and spontaneous preterm birth among Black women in the NuMom2b study
papers.abstract: ImportancePreterm birth is a leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality and disproportionately affects Black birthing people in the United States. DNA methylation-based measures of biological aging may capture physiologic dysregulation relevant to birth timing. We aim to determine whether maternal epigenetic age acceleration in early pregnancy is associated with gestational duration, spontaneous preterm birth (sPTB), and small for gestational age (SGA) among Black nulliparous pregnant individuals. MethodsThis is a secondary data analysis of the prospective, multicenter Nulliparous Pregnancy Outcomes Study: Monitoring Mothers-to-Be (nuMoM2b). Participants enrolled in eight US clinical research sites from 2010 to 2014 were followed through delivery; DNAm arrays were processed in 2024, and the current analysis was conducted in 2026. Participants were nulliparous individuals with singleton pregnancies who self-identified as Black. Maternal peripheral blood DNA methylation was measured at 6-13 weeks gestation using the Illumina MethylationEPIC array. The primary aging metric was standardized GrimAge2 age acceleration. Principal Components versions of the Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge, and DNAmTL clocks, and DunedinPACE, were used in additional analyses. Delivery data was abstracted from medical records in the NuMom2b study. Outcomes were gestational duration in days, based on the best obstetric estimate, adjudicated sPTB before 37 completed weeks, and SGA. Primary linear and logistic regression models adjusted for maternal age, smoking, gestational age at blood draw, and estimated blood cell composition. Secondary models added education and body mass index (BMI) as additional covariates. Fetal sex interaction effects were tested. ResultsAmong 931 participants (mean age = 23.46 [SD=5.33] years), 55 (5.9%) experienced sPTB. Each 1-SD higher GrimAge2 acceleration was associated with 1.32 fewer days of gestation ({beta}, -1.32 days; 95% CI, -2.36 to -0.28; P=.01) and higher odds of sPTB (odds ratio, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.13-2.02; P=.01). Results were slightly attenuated but remained significant for sPTB when controlling for education and BMI. Epigenetic age acceleration was not associated with SGA. Results were not significantly different by fetal sex. Conclusions and RelevanceGreater first-trimester maternal GrimAge2 acceleration was associated with shorter gestation and 51% higher odds of sPTB but was not associated with SGA among Black nulliparous participants. The association with sPTB persisted after adjustment for socioeconomic and metabolic characteristics, warranting further evaluation of whether GrimAge2 improves early-pregnancy prediction of sPTB value beyond these factors.
